title: Best Haul Without Neighbours
statement:
A row of stalls stands along a street. Stall i holds nums[i] coins. You may empty any set of stalls, but never two stalls that stand next to each other: emptying stalls i and i + 1 trips an alarm.

Return the largest number of coins you can collect. Taking no stalls at all (0 coins) is allowed.

examples.why: Stalls 1 and 4: 9 + 8. Taking every other stall gives only 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 or 9 + 3 = 12.
The first and last stall, with a gap of two between them. A gap can be longer than one stall.
Grabbing the biggest stall first (6) blocks both 5s.

hints: Look at the last stall. Either you take it, or you do not. What does each choice leave you with?
If you take stall i, stall i − 1 is off limits, so the rest comes from stalls 0..i − 2. If you skip it, the rest comes from stalls 0..i − 1.
Let best(i) be the most you can take from stalls 0..i. best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + nums[i]). Keep two running values.

explain.intuition:
Greedy rules like "every other stall" or "biggest first" fail, as the examples show. What works is a decision at each stall, made with the best answers for shorter streets already known.

State: best(i) = the most coins from stalls 0..i only. Recurrence: for stall i, either skip it and keep best(i − 1), or take it, which rules out stall i − 1 and adds nums[i] to best(i − 2). So best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + nums[i]). It does not matter whether best(i − 1) actually used stall i − 1: it is the best for that prefix either way. Base cases: best(−1) = 0 (no stalls) and best(0) = nums[0].
steps: State: best(i) = most coins from stalls 0..i without taking two neighbours.
Recurrence: best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + nums[i]): skip stall i, or take it.
Base cases: best(−2) = best(−1) = 0, which makes best(0) = nums[0].
Fill left to right with two variables: prev2 (best two stalls back) and prev1 (best one stall back).
pitfalls: Comparing only the even-index sum and the odd-index sum. On [2, 9, 4, 3, 8] that gives 14, but 9 + 8 = 17 skips two stalls in a row.
Writing best(i) = best(i − 2) + nums[i] without the skip option. Then the answer for a prefix is forced to use its last stall.
Updating the two variables in the wrong order, so prev2 is overwritten before it is used. Compute the new value first, then shift.

solutions.title: Plain recursion
solutions.idea: best(i) = max(skip, take) straight from the recurrence, with no cache. Exponential.

solutions.title: Table, bottom-up
solutions.idea: dp[i + 1] holds best(i); dp[0] = 0 stands for the empty street. Fill left to right.
